page.name: One-time passwords
page.h1: Send one-time passwords without the queue
page.metaDescription: Deliver OTP codes with per-number pacing, a written record of every send, and routing across accounts when one stops accepting traffic.
page.lede: Your login depends on a code landing before the session expires. Connect the accounts you already pay for and the platform paces each code to the number it leaves from — so a burst of logins drains at the speed your numbers allow instead of queueing behind one shared quota.

sections.h: Make the code impossible to misread
bullets: The code itself, in a form that cannot be misread
What the code is for, so a surprise code is recognizable as a mistake
An instruction not to share it
p: Keep it short. A longer message is more segments, and in verification the cost is not the interesting problem — the length is, because people read codes under time pressure.

sections.h: Pace the burst to the number it leaves from
p: Because provider limits apply per sender number, a burst of logins can queue behind itself. Pacing is applied at the number, and a second number raises the ceiling rather than splitting the same allowance — which is why capacity planning for OTP starts with how many numbers you own, not with which plan you are on.
bullets: Per-number pacing rather than one shared application quota
Routing across connected accounts when one stops accepting traffic
Delivery receipt status recorded against the send
Do not put anything else in the same message — a code plus a promotion reads as spam
Do not depend on delivery as proof of the person; the code is the proof
Do not retry blindly — a retried request sends a second code, because the send API has no idempotency key

faq.q: Can a code be delivered twice by accident?
faq.a: Yes, if the caller retries. There is no idempotency key on the send API, so duplicate prevention has to live in the service that calls it.

faq.q: Will an opt-out stop verification codes?
faq.a: No. Suppression is applied to promotional traffic; transactional sends such as a code are not suppressed by the same rule.

faq.q: How fast can OTP traffic go?
faq.a: As fast as the numbers you own allow. The provider’s limit is per number, and adding numbers is what raises throughput.
